stories.headline: Tens of thousands ordered to evacuate in Nevada as fire threatens Reno

opening: Tens of ⁠thousands of people have been ⁠evacuated this weekend from the ⁠area of Reno, Nevada, and many others were under orders to leave on Sunday as a wildfire reached the outskirts of the state’s third-most-populous city.

About 42,000 residents have been displaced or are under active evacuations with an additional 45,000 ‌in “be prepared to evacuate” status as the Hawk Fire threatened northern Reno, local officials said late on Sunday morning.

stories.title: Matcha, with a twist of Assam: India enters the global matcha production line
stories.summary: India's Assam region has produced its first commercial batch of matcha, using a local tea variety processed with Japanese machinery, marking a new frontier in India's 200-year-old tea industry. The Jalans, tea estate owners, overcame challenges in cultivar selection and processing to create 'Matcha assamica,' a smoother, less bitter matcha variant aimed at new global markets. This innovation reflects India's tea industry's diversification amid challenges, with matcha production seen as a promising new revenue stream supported by India-Japan collaboration and growing global demand. CHOTA TINGRAI, Assam – When Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi made her first official visit to India from July 1 to 3, a host of big-ticket agreements were announced spanning artificial intelligence, energy, defence and critical minerals. But away from this spotlight, another development – a welcome coincidence not part of the official proceedings – sprang forth on July 3 through a special India-Japan collaboration. That day, the Guwahati Tea Auction Centre in India’s north-eastern Assam state sold the country’s first commercial batch of matcha, a green tea traditionally made from shade-grown Camellia sinensis leaves in Japan. This tea, however, was made from an indigenous variety grown locally and processed using Japanese machinery in Chota Tingrai, a tea estate in Assam that has nudged India’s 200-plus-year-old tea industry into a new frontier. Black tea has long been the mainstay of the country’s tea industry, but thanks to Chota Tingrai, India is today among a handful of countries and regions other than Japan – including China, Taiwan, South Korea and Vietnam – that can produce matcha locally. The development comes as global demand for matcha has skyrocketed in recent years, driven by its claimed health benefits, growing interest in Japanese culture and the rise of cafes that seem to be folding matcha into practically every other item on their menu, ranging from lattes to doughnuts. India is no exception. Here, the vivid green swirl has found its way into traditional sweets such as ladoo and even savoury classics such as dosa. Matcha mania has sent prices zooming up globally, drawing interest from tea growers in different countries, including the Jalan family in India.

This innovation reflects India's tea industry's diversification amid challenges, with matcha production seen as a promising new revenue stream supported by India-Japan collaboration and growing global demand.
